items.prompt: What is a prediction?

options.why: That is a result. A prediction comes before the test.
Tools measure things. A prediction is an idea.
A list of materials tells you what you need, not what will happen.

hints: You make a prediction before you start a test.
It is your best guess.
Ask: do you know the answer yet when you predict?
items.explanation: A prediction is what you think will happen. You make it before the test, then check it against your results.

items.prompt: Which tool measures how long a pencil is?

options.why: A thermometer measures temperature.
A measuring jug measures liquids.
A timer measures time.

hints: How long something is, is called its length.
Which tool has centimetres marked along it?
Think about the tool in your pencil case.
items.explanation: A ruler measures length. We read the length in centimetres.

items.prompt: Match each tool to what it measures.
hints: Think about what each tool is used for.
Look at the units: cm, °C, ml and seconds.
Start with the ruler. Which unit is on a ruler?
items.explanation: A ruler measures length in centimetres, a thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius, a jug measures water in millilitres and a timer measures time in seconds.

items.prompt: Sari tests which paper towel soaks up the most water. What must she keep the same?

figure.alt: Two kinds of paper towel and some water.

options.why: That is the thing she is testing, so it changes.

options.text: the amount of water for each towel

options.why: To be fair, everything except the towel must stay the same.
That is the result she will find out.

hints: She is testing the towels, so the towels change.
Everything else must be the same for each towel.
Ask: what would make the test unfair if it was different?
items.explanation: Sari changes only the kind of towel. She keeps the amount of water the same, so the test is fair.

items.prompt: In a fair test, how many things should you change?

options.why: If you change everything, you cannot tell what made the difference.
If nothing changes, there is nothing to test.
With two changes, you cannot tell which one made the difference.

hints: A fair test helps you find out what made a difference.
If two things change, which one caused the result?
Ask: how many things can you blame for a change?
items.explanation: In a fair test you change just one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know that one thing caused any difference.

items.prompt: How long is the leaf?

figure.alt: A leaf next to a ruler. It starts at 0 and ends at 7 cm.

hints: Check that the leaf starts at 0.
Look at where the leaf ends.
Read the number on the ruler at the tip of the leaf.
items.explanation: The leaf starts at 0 and ends at 7, so it is 7 cm long.

items.prompt: Children counted minibeasts in the school garden. How many more ants than snails did they find?

figure.alt: Tally chart of minibeasts: ants 12, ladybirds 5, snails 7, worms 3.

hints: Find the ants row and the snails row.
Count each tally in groups of 5.
Ants are 12. Take away the number of snails.
items.explanation: They found 12 ants and 7 snails. 12 take away 7 is 5, so they found 5 more ants.

items.prompt: Look at the bar chart. Which ball bounced highest?

figure.title: Bounce height
figure.alt: Bar chart of bounce height: tennis ball 55 cm, rubber ball 70 cm, ping-pong ball 40 cm, football 45 cm.

options.why: The tennis ball bounced 55 cm. Another ball bounced higher.
The ping-pong ball bounced 40 cm, the lowest.
The football bounced 45 cm. Another ball bounced higher.

hints: Highest bounce means the tallest bar.
Compare the tops of the bars.
Read the number at the top of the tallest bar.
items.explanation: The rubber ball has the tallest bar, at 70 cm. It bounced highest.

items.prompt: How much higher did the rubber ball bounce than the football?

figure.title: Bounce height
figure.alt: Bar chart of bounce height: tennis ball 55 cm, rubber ball 70 cm, ping-pong ball 40 cm, football 45 cm.

hints: Find the rubber ball bar and the football bar.
Read the height of each bar.
Start with 70 cm and take away the football's height.
items.explanation: The rubber ball bounced 70 cm and the football bounced 45 cm. 70 take away 45 is 25, so the rubber ball bounced 25 cm higher.

items.prompt: Put the steps of an investigation in order.
hints: Every investigation starts with something you want to know.
You predict before you test.
Start with the question. What do you do before testing?
items.explanation: Ask a question, make a prediction, do a fair test, record the results and then say what you found out.

items.prompt: Why do scientists repeat a measurement?

options.text: to make the test take longer
options.why: Repeating helps you check your results.

options.text: to get a very different answer each time
options.why: Similar answers each time show the result can be trusted.

options.text: to check the result is right
because the first result never counts
options.why: The first result counts. Repeating helps check it.

hints: Sometimes a measurement goes wrong by accident.
If you get the same answer twice, how sure are you?
Ask: what would you do if one result looked strange?
items.explanation: Repeating a measurement checks the result. If the answers are close each time, we can trust them more.

items.prompt: Wulan wants to know if plants grow better with more water. Which plan is fair?

options.text: One plant in the sun with lots of water, one in the dark with a little.
options.why: Two things change, light and water. She cannot tell which one mattered.

options.text: Two different kinds of plant with the same water.
options.why: The water is the same, so this does not test water.

options.text: Just one plant with lots of water.
options.why: With one plant, there is nothing to compare.

options.text: The same kind of plant in the same place, but one gets more water.

hints: She is testing water, so only the water should change.
Check each plan. How many things are different?
Look for the plan where everything is the same except the water.
items.explanation: The fair plan uses the same kind of plant in the same place and changes only the water. Then any difference must come from the water.

items.prompt: Galih counts birds at the feeder. How many birds came on Monday and Wednesday altogether?

figure.title: Birds at the feeder
figure.alt: Pictogram of birds at the feeder. Each bird symbol means 2 birds. Monday 4 symbols, Tuesday 6 symbols, Wednesday 3 symbols.

hints: Read the key. Each symbol means 2 birds.
Work out Monday, then Wednesday.
Monday has 4 symbols. Count in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8.
items.explanation: Monday has 4 symbols, which is 8 birds. Wednesday has 3 symbols, which is 6 birds. 8 and 6 make 14 birds.

items.prompt: Look at the results. What can you conclude?

figure.caption: Ice cubes melting
head: Place
Minutes to melt
figure.alt: Table of ice cubes melting: fridge 90 minutes, classroom 30 minutes, sunny window 12 minutes.

options.text: Ice melts faster where it is colder.
options.why: The fridge was coldest, and the ice there took the longest.

options.text: Ice melts faster where it is warmer.
Ice melts at the same speed everywhere.
options.why: The times are different in each place.

options.text: Ice does not melt in a classroom.
options.why: It melted in 30 minutes in the classroom.

hints: Which place is the warmest? Which is the coldest?
Fewer minutes means the ice melted faster.
Compare the sunny window with the fridge.
items.explanation: The ice melted in 12 minutes by the warm sunny window and took 90 minutes in the cold fridge. Ice melts faster where it is warmer.

items.prompt: Bayu predicted the big ball would bounce highest. The small ball bounced highest. What should he do?

options.text: Change the results to match his prediction.
options.why: Results must be written down honestly, even when they surprise us.
Surprising results are still useful.

options.text: Say his prediction was wrong and explain the results.

options.why: A surprising result can show something new. The test can still be fair.

hints: Predictions are allowed to be wrong.
Scientists always record what really happened.
Ask: which choice is honest about the results?
items.explanation: A prediction can be wrong, and that is fine. Bayu should record the real results, say his prediction was wrong and explain what he found.

items.prompt: Mei tests which material keeps an ice cube frozen longest. Sort the cards.

items.text: the size of the ice cube

hints: She is testing materials.
Only the thing being tested should change.
Ask for each card: would changing it make the test unfair?
items.explanation: Mei changes only the material round the ice. She keeps the ice size, the place and the checking times the same, so the test is fair.

items.prompt: Draw a table to record how high 3 balls bounce. Fill it in with your results.

criteria.label: Draws a table with two columns and a heading for each
Lists 3 balls in the first column
Writes a height with cm for each ball

hints: Write Ball at the top of the first column and Height at the top of the second.
Measure each bounce with a ruler or a metre stick, with a helper.
items.explanation: A table keeps results tidy. Each row shows one ball and how high it bounced, in centimetres.

items.prompt: Kai tested two paper towels. He poured the same amount of water onto each one. Towel A soaked up 12 drops and towel B soaked up 8 drops.
hints: A fair test changes only one thing.
Look at what Kai kept the same.
Subtract the smaller number from the larger number.
items.explanation: Kai changed the kind of towel and kept the amount of water the same. 12 take away 8 is 4, so towel A soaked up 4 more drops.

parts.prompt: What did Kai keep the same?
How many more drops did towel A soak up than towel B?

items.prompt: A plant in the light grows 2 cm every day. Complete the table.
hints: Look at how the height changes from one day to the next.
Add 2 each day.
Day 3 is 6 cm. What is Day 4?
items.explanation: The plant grows 2 cm each day: 2, 4, 6, 8 cm.
items.caption: Plant in the light
head: Day
Height (cm)

items.prompt: Write a table of your own results on paper. Use two columns, Day and Height, for a bean plant. Then take a photo.
hints: Draw a table with two columns.
Write Day in the first column heading.
items.explanation: A good results table has clear headings and numbers in rows.

items.prompt: What is a fair test?

options.text: A test where only one thing is changed.
A test where everything is changed.
options.why: Then we cannot tell what made the difference.
We should measure.
A fair test is about keeping things the same.

hints: Think about changing one thing.
Everything else must stay the same.
It is fair to all.
items.explanation: In a fair test we change one thing and keep everything else the same.

items.prompt: Which tool measures how heavy something is?

options.why: A ruler measures length.
A clock tells the time.
A thermometer measures heat.

hints: It is not for length.
You put things on it.
It tells you grams or kilograms.
items.explanation: We use scales to measure how heavy something is.

items.prompt: Which tool measures how much water is in a jug?

options.why: A ruler measures length.
A clock tells the time.
Scales measure weight.

hints: It has lines on the side.
It holds liquid.
It is for water.
items.explanation: A measuring jug has lines that show how many millilitres of liquid it holds.

items.prompt: Dewi tests which paper holds the most coins. What should she change?

options.why: The coins must be the same.
The paper size must be the same.
The table must be the same.

hints: What is she testing?
Change only that.
Keep the coins the same.
items.explanation: She is testing paper, so she changes the type of paper. Everything else stays the same.

items.prompt: Raj tests which ball bounces highest. What must stay the same?

options.why: This is what he changes.

options.text: the height he drops the balls from

options.why: This is what he changes.
This does not matter.

hints: What does Raj change?
Keep everything else the same.
The height matters.
items.explanation: The drop height must stay the same for a fair test. He only changes the ball.

items.prompt: What is the best way to record results?

options.why: You may forget.
A table is easier to read.
A table shows numbers.

hints: You need to look back later.
Rows and columns help.
Write it down.
items.explanation: A table keeps the numbers neat, so we can compare them easily.

items.prompt: Kai gives plant food to plant A but not to plant B. Plant A grows taller. What can Kai say?

options.text: Plant A grew taller with plant food.
Plant food always makes plants taller.
options.why: One test cannot prove always.

options.text: Plant B did not need water.
options.why: Both plants needed water.

options.text: Plants grow better in the dark.
options.why: The test was not about light.

hints: Say only what you saw.
Do not say always.
Compare A and B.
items.explanation: Kai can only say what he found: plant A grew taller with plant food.

items.prompt: Paper towel test: what changes and what stays the same?
hints: What are we testing?
Only one thing changes.
The rest must be fair.
items.explanation: We change only the type of towel. The amount of water, the size and the waiting time stay the same.

items.prompt: Which stay the same when we test surfaces for a rolling car?
hints: Only the surface changes.
Use the same car.
The ramp is the same.
items.explanation: To test the surface fairly, keep the car, ramp height and starting point the same.

items.prompt: Put the steps of a fair test in order.
hints: Plan before you test.
Record while you test.
Look at the results last.
items.explanation: Choose what to change and keep other things the same. Then do the test, measure and record, and look at the results.

items.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: say what you think will happen
find how much or how long
say how things are the same or different
hints: Predict comes before the test.
Record is to write.
Compare looks at two things.
items.explanation: To predict is to say what will happen. To measure is to find how much. To record is to write down. To compare is to see what is the same or different.

items.prompt: In a fair test we change ___ thing. We keep the other things the ___.
hints: How many things do we change?
The rest should not change.
Read slowly.
items.explanation: In a fair test we change one thing and keep the other things the same.

Bounce (cm)

Take 25 from 50.
Towel B soaked up 25.

This is what he changes.
